definition.text: Seventeen global goals that all UN members adopted in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

facts.text: The 17 goals come with 169 measurable targets and link the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development.
The SDGs are universal, time-bound and legally non-binding policy objectives agreed by governments.
Each goal typically has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, averaging 1.5 indicators per target.
Three goals focus on the environment: SDG 13 (climate), SDG 14 (oceans) and SDG 15 (land), but there is no overarching planetary goal.
On 25 September 2015 the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted the agenda titled 'Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'.
The SDGs succeeded the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015; critics note there are many more goals than the eight MDGs.
A 2024 UN report found only 17% of SDG targets on track; the 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress and 18% were in reverse.
Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten progress, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed it.

definition.text: Indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track progress towards each SDG target.

facts.text: Targets are either outcome targets, numbered (6.1), or means-of-implementation targets, lettered (6.a).
For each indicator an expert group tried to name a custodian agency responsible for methods, data collection and reporting.
Critics worry about the large number of indicators and the cost of monitoring them, estimated in the billions of dollars.
The UN High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development monitors the SDGs, and countries can file voluntary national reviews of their progress.

title: Trade-offs among the SDGs

definition.text: The concern that pursuing some SDGs can work against others, so that not all 17 can be reached together.

facts.text: Cited examples: reconciling ending hunger, economic growth and income equality with environmental sustainability.
Critics say the SDGs rely on dubious claims about decoupling and resource efficiency instead of addressing the tension between growth and sustainability.
Synergies also exist: the IPCC sees robust synergies between climate action and the goals on health, clean energy, cities, consumption and oceans.
Countries tend to prioritize socioeconomic goals over environmental ones, and SDGs 1 and 8 were found to be most widely prioritized.

contested_note: Scholars disagree whether the goals are internally coherent or contain inherently conflicting targets.

title: SDGs weak on environmental sustainability
article: Sustainable Development Goals#Weak on environmental sustainability

definition.text: The criticism that the SDGs treat economic growth as foundational and do not make protecting the Earth system an end in itself.

facts.text: Environmental constraints and planetary boundaries are underrepresented, and the SDGs do not pursue planetary integrity as such.
Even within the environment-focused goals, most indicators measure social or economic outcomes.
Some studies argue that planetary integrity and justice would require limits to economic growth.
A 2022 meta-analysis of over 3,000 articles found the SDGs have had only limited transformative political impact.

contested_note: Environmentalists call for redefining sustainable development in the SDGs, against their growth-centred design.

definition.text: Estimates of how much money reaching the SDGs would take, and where it might come from.

facts.text: In 2014 UNCTAD estimated the cost of reaching the goals at US$2.5 trillion per year.
A 2020 estimate put the financing gap in developing countries at US$2.5 trillion per year before COVID-19, projected to rise to US$4.2 trillion in 2020.
The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda is one UN process for financing the SDGs, and private investment is seen as essential.
Blended finance is designed to support progress towards the SDGs.

definition.text: A multilateral treaty, known informally as the Biodiversity Convention, for conserving the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It has three main goals: conserving biodiversity, using its components sustainably, and sharing fairly the benefits from genetic resources.
It opened for signature at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.
As of 2016 it had 196 Parties; the United States is the only UN member state that has not ratified it, citing sovereignty and economic interests.
It has two supplementary agreements, the Cartagena Protocol on biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on benefit-sharing.
Its regulated issues include access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge, with prior informed consent of the providing party.
The idea was conceived at a UNEP expert working group in November 1988; its Secretariat in Montreal operates under UNEP.
Its Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020 contained the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, later followed by the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework.

title: CBD Conference of the Parties
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Conference of the Parties (COP)

definition.text: The governing body of the Biodiversity Convention, made up of all governments that have ratified it.

facts.text: It reviews progress, sets priorities and work plans, and can amend the Convention and create expert advisory bodies.
COP met yearly for three years after 1994 and then every two years; COP 1 was in Nassau, Bahamas.
A scientific expert committee, the SBSTTA, advises the COP on scientific and technical issues.
COP 15, planned for Kunming in 2020, was postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic and split into two sessions.

title: Aichi Biodiversity Targets
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020

definition.text: Twenty international targets for 2011–2020, set under the Biodiversity Convention, to protect biodiversity, species and sustainable use of resources.

facts.text: They were part of the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020, agreed at COP 10 in Nagoya in October 2010, and addressed five strategic goals.
Goal A sought to tackle the underlying causes of biodiversity loss by mainstreaming biodiversity across government and society.
Other goals aimed to cut direct pressures, safeguard ecosystems, species and genetic diversity, and enhance benefits from ecosystem services.
Countries failed to meet them because they lacked clarity, were hard to measure, went unreported and had limited funding.
The CBD mapped synergies between the 17 SDGs and the 20 Aichi targets.

title: Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Marine and coastal biodiversity

definition.text: Ocean areas identified under the Biodiversity Convention, using scientific criteria, as especially important for marine life.

facts.text: Expert workshops from 2018 to 2022 explored options for revising EBSA descriptions and describing new areas.
The aim is an international legally binding instrument under UNCLOS for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, the High Seas Treaty.

title: Criticism of the Biodiversity Convention

definition.text: Arguments that the Biodiversity Convention has been weakly enforced and unfair to biodiversity-rich poorer countries.

facts.text: Brazil argued that wealthier countries benefit from access to resources but give too little financial and technological support for conservation.
The CBD is described as a hard treaty gone soft, and countries face no penalties for ignoring it.
National strategies in practice neglect groups such as fungi, bacteria and protists.
Some scientists fear the Nagoya Protocol hampers disease prevention and conservation research.

contested_note: Developing countries and critics dispute whether richer nations have met their obligations under the Convention.

title: IPBES
article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

definition.text: An independent intergovernmental body, set up by governments in 2012, that links biodiversity science to policy-making.

facts.text: It plays a role similar to the IPCC, but besides assessments it also builds knowledge, capacity and policy support tools.
A 2010 UN General Assembly resolution asked UNEP to convene a meeting to establish it; its members meet in Plenaries every one to two years.
Its 2019 Global Assessment, adopted by representatives of 132 members in Paris, was the largest study to date of biodiversity and ecosystem services.
A 2020 IPBES report said preventing pandemics through conservation is more cost-effective than responding after outbreaks.
IPBES and the IPCC shared the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity in October 2022.
In January 2026 the United States announced its withdrawal from IPBES.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
sources.key: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: Biodiversity and climate change nexus
article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Cooperation with IPCC

definition.text: The idea, set out in a joint IPBES–IPCC report, that climate change and biodiversity loss are linked and must be tackled together.

facts.text: In June 2021 IPBES and the IPCC released a co-sponsored workshop report on biodiversity and climate change.
Efforts to address one problem can worsen the other if their links are overlooked.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
sources.key: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: IPBES Transformative Change Assessment
article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Transformative Change Assessment

definition.text: An IPBES report, approved on 18 December 2024, on the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and how to bring about transformative change.

facts.text: It builds on the 2019 Global Assessment, which found that only transformative change can achieve global development goals.
The 2019 assessment also warned that society should not focus solely on economic growth given the loss of biodiversity.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
sources.key: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: IPBES Nexus Assessment
article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Nexus Assessment

definition.text: An IPBES report, approved on 17 December 2024, on how biodiversity, water, food and health are connected.

facts.text: It looks for ways to maximise benefits across five nexus elements: biodiversity, water, food, health and climate change.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
sources.key: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework

definition.text: The global plan for nature adopted at the 2022 UN Biodiversity Conference (COP15) under the Biodiversity Convention.

facts.text: It was adopted on 19 December 2022 and promoted as a 'Paris Agreement for Nature'; it is the most significant CBD agreement to date.
It contains four global goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030, and succeeds the Strategic Plan 2011–2020 with its Aichi targets.
Goal A aims to cut the extinction rate and risk of all species tenfold by 2050 and halt human-induced extinction of threatened species.
Target 3, the '30 by 30' target, asks governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and water area by 2030.
Countries are also to stop subsidising activities that destroy wilderness, such as mining and industrial fishing.
Target 13 commits parties to share fairly the benefits from genetic resources and digital sequence information.
It is not legally binding, and its targets are criticised as vague, lacking measurable indicators; by COP16 only 44 of 196 parties had new biodiversity plans.
It is named after Kunming, the original host city, and Montreal, which hosted COP15 after Kunming withdrew because of China's COVID policy.

contested_note: Critics, including the IPBES chair, warn it may yield business as usual because its targets are vague and non-binding.
distinct_from: GBF implications for business and finance

title: GBF implications for business and finance

definition.text: Expected effects of the global biodiversity framework on companies, banks and central banks, according to the UNEP Finance Initiative.

facts.text: Companies are expected to face mandatory disclosure of their impacts on biodiversity.
Banks are expected to shift money into nature-restoring projects, and central banks to treat nature-loss risk as part of their mandates.
Nature-positive, the goal of halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, has helped mainstream the framework in business and governance.
In May 2024 UNEP and China launched the Kunming Biodiversity Fund, with China committing $230 million USD.

definition.text: Sites outside formal protected areas that are governed and managed in ways that conserve biodiversity in place over the long term.

facts.text: Unlike protected areas, OECMs need not be dedicated to conservation, but must deliver effective long-term conservation of biodiversity.
The term first appeared in Aichi Target 11 in 2010, which sought to conserve 17% of land and inland waters and 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020.
The CBD formalised the definition in 2018 through Decision 14/8 at COP 14, building on Canadian guidelines and IUCN advice.
OECMs count towards Target 3 of the Global Biodiversity Framework.
As of June 2026, 7,488 OECM sites cover 1.31% of Earth's surface, about 1.1% on land and 0.21% at sea.
They allow small-scale uses such as fisheries and low-impact agroforestry and aim to be more equitable than protected areas, which have caused displacement.
Locally managed marine areas are one form of OECM.

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life below water': to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.

facts.text: It has ten targets, covering marine pollution, ecosystem protection, ocean acidification, sustainable fishing and conserving coastal and marine areas.
Target 14.5 aimed to conserve at least 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020, measured by protected-area coverage.
Target 14.4 is measured by the share of fish stocks within biologically sustainable levels.
Ocean pH now averages 8.1, about 30% more acidic than in pre-industrial times.
Sustainable fisheries made up roughly 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017.
Oceans cover over 70% of Earth's surface, yet from 2013 to 2021 only 1.1% of national research budgets went to ocean science.
The World Economic Forum estimates US$175 billion a year of blue finance is needed to achieve SDG 14.

title: Harmful fisheries subsidies
article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Target 14.6: End subsidies contributing to overfishing

definition.text: Government payments to fishing fleets that encourage overcapacity, overfishing or illegal fishing, which SDG Target 14.6 aims to end.

facts.text: Capacity-enhancing subsidies help developing countries compete with large fishing nations, but bring no long-term benefit if they cause overfishing.
The WWF estimates illegal fishing costs up to $36.4 billion a year globally.
The Global Biodiversity Framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidising destructive activities such as industrial fishing.

title: Large-scale marine protected areas
article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Large-Scale Marine Protected Areas (LSMPAs)

definition.text: Marine protected areas of at least 100,000 square km, set up to cut overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems.

facts.text: Concerns about them span resource management, conflicts between rival countries, and trade-offs between people's needs and the environment.
The management challenge is inadequate monitoring and enforcement of protection measures.

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life on land': to protect, restore and sustainably use land ecosystems, manage forests, combat desertification and halt biodiversity loss.

facts.text: It has 12 targets to be achieved by 2030, measured by 14 indicators.
Outcome targets include ending deforestation, restoring degraded land, protecting habitats and sharing benefits from genetic resources fairly.
Forests cover roughly 4 billion hectares, or 30.7 per cent of the world's land; 93 percent are natural and 7 percent planted.
Target 15.5 on threatened species is measured by the Red List Index.
Target 15.9 asks countries to build ecosystem and biodiversity values into national planning and accounts.
As of 2023 there was about a $700 billion gap in financial support for low-income countries to protect biodiversity.
Deforestation is estimated to have risen by 12% from 2019 to 2020.

title: Illegal wildlife trade targets
article: Sustainable Development Goal 15#Target 15.c: Combat global poaching and trafficking

definition.text: SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and tackle both demand and supply of illegal wildlife products.

facts.text: Illegal wildlife trade has become one of the world's largest black markets, valued at tens of billions of dollars.
Trade policies that reward sustainable use typically help wildlife populations faster than outright trade bans.
Trafficking is usually driven by organised crime and eased by corruption and weak governance.

title: 30 by 30

definition.text: A global initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean area by 2030.

facts.text: It was proposed in a 2019 Science Advances article, 'A Global Deal for Nature', partly to help mitigate climate change.
Launched by the High Ambition Coalition in 2020, it had more than 100 supporting countries by October 2022.
In December 2022 it became Target 3 of the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
As of May 2026, 17.3% of land and inland waters and 9.8% of marine areas were protected; counting OECMs, 18.4% and 10.0%.
Some conservationists say the 30% figure lacks clear scientific justification, while others argue it is too low and point to the Half-Earth idea of conserving about 50%.
Critics warn that broad definitions counting OECMs with intensive industrial activity could inflate reported progress.
NGOs and Indigenous groups warn it could lead to forced evictions, 'green grabbing' and green colonialism without human-rights safeguards.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether 30% is scientifically justified, too low, or a risk to Indigenous land rights.

definition.text: Protected areas that exist in law but lack the funding, staff or enforcement to stop poaching, logging or development inside them.

facts.text: Modelling suggests that for exploited species, better enforcement in existing reserves often helps more than expanding area without more resources.
Where threats such as over-harvesting are intense, spending on compliance and management can beat creating new, weakly managed reserves.
Where pressures cluster near reserve edges, enlarging protected areas can create secure core refuges even without more staff.
Meeting percentage targets without governance capacity risks spreading scarce conservation money too thin.

definition.text: The European Commission's 2020 plan for biodiversity, offered as the EU's contribution to the post-2020 global framework.

facts.text: It plans to make 30% of EU territory protected by 2030, with 10% strictly protected.
It proposed binding nature restoration targets and is a core part of the European Green Deal.
As of 2023 the EU was not on track to meet its targets.

definition.text: A 2010 supplementary agreement to the Biodiversity Convention on access to genetic resources and fair sharing of the benefits from their use.

facts.text: It implements the CBD's third objective, the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
Adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, it entered into force on 12 October 2014; by August 2025 it had 142 parties.
It gives each country sovereign rights over its biological resources, making biopiracy illegal.
Access requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms; benefits may be monetary or non-monetary, such as royalties or shared research results.
It also covers traditional knowledge linked to genetic resources, which cannot be accessed without permission from the communities holding it.
Users must monitor genetic resources after they leave a country through checkpoints along the value chain, from research to commercialisation.
Marine genetic resources from the high seas fall outside its benefit-sharing regime, because it covers only national jurisdiction.

title: Criticism of the Nagoya Protocol

definition.text: Concerns that the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy harms biodiversity research, conservation and disease response.

facts.text: Some developing countries have refused permits for basic biodiversity research and even prosecuted scientists.
Its bilateral transfer system has low throughput, whereas the plant genetic resources treaty's multilateral system allows 8500 transfers every week.
Lack of national implementation is often blamed for the protocol's failure.

contested_note: Scientists and museums see the protocol as red tape, while providers of genetic resources defend it as protection against biopiracy.

definition.text: A place that is protected because of its recognised natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited.

facts.text: The IUCN defines it as a clearly defined space managed, by legal or other effective means, for the long-term conservation of nature and its ecosystem services.
As of 2016 over 161,000 protected areas covered about 17 percent of the world's land surface, excluding Antarctica.
14,688 marine protected areas cover about 10.2% of coastal and marine areas and 4.12% of the global ocean.
Protecting biodiversity in them also protects ecosystem services such as water, fuel, carbon sequestration and climate regulation.
Under Article 8 of the Biodiversity Convention, parties agreed to establish a system of protected areas.
Protecting places is not new: over 2000 years ago royal decrees in India protected certain areas.
New restrictions can displace local people, souring relations with conservationists and sometimes driving poaching.

title: IUCN protected area categories
article: Protected area#IUCN Protected Area Management Categories

definition.text: Six categories, set by the IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas, that classify protected areas by their management objectives.

facts.text: They provide international standards for defining protected areas and are recognised by many governments and the UN.
They range from Category Ia, strict nature reserve, and Category II, national park, to Category VI, protected areas with sustainable use of natural resources.

definition.text: How well protected areas actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for example by comparing populations inside and outside them.

facts.text: Vertebrate populations declined about five times more slowly inside protected areas (−0.4% per year) than at similar unprotected sites (−1.8% per year).
Effectiveness is limited by small size, isolation, high costs and growing conflict with human demands for resources.
Only 18% of the area covered by protected areas has been assessed, so most of them have unclear effectiveness.

definition.text: The UN goal 'Climate action': to take urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts.

facts.text: It has five targets for 2030, including strengthening resilience to climate disasters and building climate measures into national policy.
Target 13.a refers to developed countries' commitment to mobilise $100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C, but pledges would still lead to about 2.7 °C by 2100.
Indicator 13.2.1 counts countries with nationally determined contributions and adaptation plans.
COVID-19 cut 2020 emissions about 6% below projections, but the fall was only temporary.
Critics say it overlooks climate migration as an adaptive response.

definition.text: A global conservation target to halt, or significantly slow, the decline of biodiversity by the end of 2010.

facts.text: EU leaders first adopted it at Gothenburg in June 2001; in 2002 the CBD's COP 6 committed to a significant reduction in the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.
The 2002 Johannesburg World Summit on Sustainable Development confirmed the target.
Measuring the rate of biodiversity loss to check the target proved a challenge.
The world largely failed to meet it; 2010's 110 national reports showed little progress.

definition.text: A national or local program for protecting and restoring threatened species and habitats, prepared under the Biodiversity Convention.

facts.text: The concept emerged from the 1992 Biodiversity Convention, which asked nations to develop strategies for conserving biodiversity.
A typical plan inventories species or habitats, assesses their conservation status, sets targets, and lays out budgets, timelines and partners.
Plans can focus on species, habitats or agricultural production.
As of 2009, 191 countries had ratified the CBD, but only some had produced comprehensive plans.
A country plan may cost up to 100 million pounds sterling, with yearly upkeep about ten percent of that, which strains poorer countries.
Critics note many plans are pro-forma and almost all overlook fungi, invertebrates and micro-organisms.
Some developing countries object that the plans put wildlife protection above food and industrial production.

definition.text: A supplement to the Biodiversity Convention that governs the movement of genetically modified organisms between countries to protect biodiversity.

facts.text: Adopted on 29 January 2000, it entered into force on 11 September 2003; by July 2020 it had 173 parties.
It rests on the precautionary principle of the 1992 Rio Declaration: lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to delay cost-effective protection.
Countries may ban imports of GMOs lacking evidence of safety, and exporters must label shipments of altered commodities such as corn or cotton.
Its Advance Informed Agreement procedure lets importing countries assess risks before the first import of an organism meant for release.
Importing countries may also weigh socio-economic considerations when deciding on imports.

title: Convention on Migratory Species
article: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals

definition.text: An international agreement, also called the Bonn Convention, to conserve migratory animals throughout their ranges.

facts.text: It was signed on 23 June 1979 in Bonn and took effect on 1 November 1983; its secretariat is run by UNEP.
Appendix I lists migratory species threatened with extinction, which range states must strictly protect.
Appendix II lists species that would benefit from international cooperation, the basis for regional or global agreements.
As a framework convention it has spawned seven agreements, such as one covering 254 wetland-dependent bird species, plus several memoranda of understanding.

sources.title: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals
sources.key: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals

definition.text: Genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources that has actual or potential value.

facts.text: They are one of the three levels of biodiversity defined by the Biodiversity Convention in 1992.
Germplasm, for example, is genetic material kept for breeding, preservation and research.
Earlier agreements treated genetic resources as common heritage; the CBD instead gave each state sovereign rights over those in its territory.
Developing countries criticised the common heritage approach for letting their resources be exploited without compensation and commercialised in industrialised nations.

title: Digital sequence information

definition.text: A placeholder policy term, used especially in the Biodiversity Convention, for data such as DNA sequences derived from genetic resources.

facts.text: It is crucial to research in public health, medicine, biodiversity, breeding and evolution.
Researchers share it freely online, which conflicts with benefit-sharing duties because users can access it without agreements.
At COP 15 in 2022 parties agreed a multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism that decouples access from benefit-sharing.
At COP 16 in 2024 they set up the Cali Fund, to which industries using DSI, such as pharma and cosmetics, are expected to contribute part of their profits.
Half of the Cali Fund is to go to local and Indigenous groups.

contested_note: The term itself remains disputed, and parties disagree over how open data should be reconciled with benefit-sharing.

definition.text: A legally binding agreement under the Law of the Sea convention to conserve and sustainably use marine life in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

facts.text: Areas beyond national jurisdiction, the high seas and the international seabed, make up about two-thirds of the ocean and were largely unregulated.
The text was adopted on 19 June 2023; Morocco's ratification on 19 September 2025 made 60, and it took effect on 17 January 2026.
It covers four elements: marine genetic resources, area-based tools including marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and capacity building.
Benefits from marine genetic resources, used in cosmetics and medicines, are to be shared, both monetary and non-monetary; fish and fishing are excluded.
Marine protected areas on the high seas can be adopted by consensus or a three-quarter majority and then bind all parties.
Parties must carry out environmental impact assessments for activities that may affect the marine environment.
Negotiations turned on the tension between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

title: Nature Restoration Law

definition.text: A 2024 European Union regulation that makes binding targets for restoring damaged nature across the EU.

facts.text: Member states must restore at least 30% of habitats in poor condition by 2030, 60% by 2040 and 90% by 2050.
It responds to more than 80% of Europe's habitats being in poor condition.
Its aims include protecting ecosystem services, mitigating climate change and reducing risks to food security.
Farm groups and the European People's Party opposed it as a threat to livelihoods; the Parliament passed it 329 to 275 and it took effect on 18 August 2024.

contested_note: Farming groups and centre-right parties opposed it as harmful to farmers, while scientists and the IUCN backed it.
notes: EU-level regulation kept as a regional example of binding restoration targets; drop if the course excludes regional laws.

definition.text: An international treaty, signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance.

facts.text: It took effect on 21 December 1975 and is also called the Convention on Wetlands.
In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres.
To join, a country had to designate at least one wetland site and guarantee its protection.
World Wetlands Day, 2 February, marks its adoption in 1971.
Domestic implementation is often half-hearted and inadequate.

title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
article: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

definition.text: An international treaty, known as UNCLOS, that sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities.

facts.text: It came out of the third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea, 1973 to 1982, and entered into force on 16 November 1994.
It replaced the 17th-century 'freedom of the seas' idea, under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation.
It set zones measured from a baseline, including exclusive economic zones extending 200 nautical miles.
Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to license seabed mining and distribute royalties.
Part XII obliges all states to cooperate in protecting the marine environment.
It has 172 parties; the United States signed but has not ratified it.
The 2023 High Seas Treaty was added because UNCLOS gave no framework for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
sources.key: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

title: Common heritage of mankind

definition.text: The principle that certain resources, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation.

facts.text: Plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage before the CBD and could be freely exchanged for breeding and research.
Developing countries criticised this approach because their resources could be exploited without compensation; the CBD replaced it with national sovereignty.
High Seas Treaty talks turned on the contrast between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

contested_note: Developing countries and industrialised nations disagree over whether genetic resources should be common heritage or sovereign property.

title: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
article: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: A UN treaty to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through long-term national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

facts.text: It defines desertification as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions caused by climate variations and human activities.
Adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and in force since December 1996, it is the only convention arising directly from the Rio Agenda 21.
It is the only legally binding international framework on desertification and has 197 parties.
National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities, are its key instruments.
Its 2018–2030 Strategic Framework includes supporting land degradation neutrality and strengthening drought resilience.
At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged for desertification, land degradation and drought.

sources.title: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
sources.key: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: A UN declaration adopted on 28 October 1982 setting out five principles of conservation to guide all human conduct affecting nature.

facts.text: Its principles include respecting nature, safeguarding genetic viability and habitats, and managing resources for sustainable productivity without endangering other species.
The vote was 111 for, one against (the United States) and 18 abstentions; the IUCN prepared it.
It gave the first international recognition to a strong form of the precautionary principle.

sources.title: International Union for Conservation of Nature
sources.key: International Union for Conservation of Nature

definition.text: A landmark or area protected under a UNESCO-run treaty because of its outstanding cultural, historical or natural value to humanity.

facts.text: The World Heritage Convention was adopted by UNESCO on 16 November 1972, took effect on 17 December 1975, and had 196 states as of November 2024.
Sites must have 'outstanding universal value' and meet at least one of ten criteria, including containing key natural habitats for conserving biodiversity.
Listing brings international recognition, legal protection, possible World Heritage Fund money, and often more tourism revenue.
Nearly three-quarters of bird species and two-thirds of mammals have been recorded at World Heritage Sites, which cover less than 1% of the planet.
Threatened sites can go on the List of World Heritage in Danger; only three have ever been delisted.
Critics point to a lobbying industry driven by tourism returns and costly bids that disadvantage poorer countries.

title: National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan

definition.text: A country's main plan for carrying out the Biodiversity Convention at home, known as an NBSAP.

facts.text: The Convention requires each country to prepare a national biodiversity strategy and build it into planning in every sector that affects biodiversity.
As of early 2012, 173 Parties had developed NBSAPs.
Countries were expected to present updated NBSAPs to meet the Kunming-Montreal targets before COP16, but only 25 of 195 had done so.
Only five of the 17 megadiverse countries and four G7 nations submitted theirs by the deadline.
Japan's 2023 NBSAP includes the aim of a nature-positive economy.

title: Half-Earth proposal

definition.text: E. O. Wilson's 2016 proposal that half of the Earth's surface be set aside as a human-free natural reserve to preserve biodiversity.

facts.text: The name 'Half-Earth' was coined for the idea by Tony Hiss; Wilson's book of that name (2016) closes a trilogy.
A Science reviewer questioned whether it was realistic, since in 2015 only 15% of land and 2.8% of marine areas were protected.
Reviewers called it more an aspirational goal than a plan, noting it gives no detail on territories, funding mechanisms or agreements, or on whether people in reserves would be relocated.

contested_note: Reviewers split on whether the target is realistic or politically workable.
